"It's humanity's first time launching multiple commercial reentry vehicles simultaneously," Varda CEO Will Bruey told Space.com on Tuesday (Oct. 7) of the Transporter-18 launch. The payloads on the Transporter-18 Varda craft ranged from pharmaceuticals to demo navigation systems to exterior thermal-protection materials. The company bills its spacecraft as mini-factories, which can host the orbital production of valuable goods such as pharmaceuticals and then bring them safely down to Earth. Another Varda vehicle is scheduled to follow them into space later this month. Assuming the third spacecraft launches nominally, all three will come down before Christmas in the Koonibba Test Range in the South Australian Outback, through coordination with Varda's long-time space-mission service provider, Southern Launch. candidates.title: Astronaut captures mesmerizing auroras with iPhone from ISS | Space photo of the day for Oct. 13, 2026
candidates.raw_excerpt: Earth's night side is wreathed in colorful auroras in a new smartphone image captured from the ISS. (Image credit: Anil Menon, NASA) NASA astronaut Anil Menon captured a gorgeous view of the northern lights dancing over the night side of Earth from the International Space Station on Oct. 10 using an iPhone camera. What is it? Menon's photo reveals spectacular pink, purple and red auroras glowing in Earth's upper atmosphere above a sparse dappling of city lights, subtly blurred by the motion of the orbital spacecraft over the course of the exposure. Bright stars glimmer between the solar panels and outer hulls of the ISS and visiting spacecraft, painted purple by the auroral display. "Flying through is rare and amazing," Menon wrote in a separate aurora video he posted to X on Oct. 10. "You can see the lights on the outside of [the] station reflecting back like Christmas LEDs. It's definitely more immersive." Why is it amazing? Menon captured the auroras during a period of heightened geomagnetic activity, after several coronal mass ejections (CMEs) struck Earth's magnetic field, triggering geomagnetic storms ranging from minor (G1) to strong (G3) over the weekend. During geomagnetic storms, more charged particles are accelerated along Earth's magnetic field lines toward the polar regions, where they collide with gases in the upper atmosphere; they excite them, causing them to release energy as light and producing spectacular auroral displays. The blue-purple colors seen in Menon's image are largely produced by nitrogen at altitudes of around 60-120 miles (100-200 kilometers) , while the red hue comes from oxygen atoms higher up, typically above 125 miles (200 kilometers). The photo is particularly impressive because it was captured on an iPhone camera, as opposed to the more traditional Nikon cameras that astronauts sometimes use to capture Earth during their time aboard the ISS. candidates.title: Kayla Bigham, FAA
candidates.raw_excerpt: Kayla Bigham grew up wanting to be an astronaut. Then, after learning about the Apollo 1 and Apollo 13 emergencies in elementary school, her goal shifted—she knew she wanted to keep space exploration safe. Bigham, 27, is now living out that dream as a flight-safety analyst at the FAA’s Office of Commercial Space Transportation. In her job, she analyzes rockets and reentry capsules looking to fly, and studies—in a worst-case scenario—how to ensure the public remains safe from space debris. “There are definitely industries—nuclear is a great example—where huge disasters have stunted an industry that otherwise could bring a lot of good,” she told Payload. “I would hate to see that happen to space.” Go boom: Bigham’s first job was investigating fire and gas explosions in the oil and gas industry, to provide evidence after a disaster. While this first job was outside the space industry, she credits the role with preparing her for the FAA. She points to a lot of overlap: the two positions are very safety-oriented, and study how failures can cause property damage and personal harm. New horizons: Working for the FAA, Bigham says every day offers a new challenge. “If I was doing design work for a company, I’d be looking at the same system on the same rocket for months,” she said. “I’m looking at every system on every rocket to get a holistic picture.”  She’s also gotten to be on the front lines of developing Part 450, the new regulations that aim to ease burdens for launchers seeking permission to fly, though these regulations have faced some criticism from industry. Bigham has a message to those who claim the government is seeking to stifle commercial space innovation. “Our entire office is very pro-commercial space. We’re doing science for pharmaceuticals, everything that patches and impacts everyday life.” Clark always had aspirations to be an aerospace engineer. Her childhood projects, like “satellites” made of coffee cans and aluminum wrapping, led to student work at California State University, Long Beach building experimental small rockets.  Clark took on internships at several name-brand companies, including Relativity Space, Blue Origin, and Vast. She also was accepted into the Zed Factor Fellowship class of 2024, and was a Brooke Owens Fellow for the class of 2026.  The big payoff: One of Clark’s favorite parts of aerospace engineering is seeing “stuff that you worked on touch space. That is such a surreal feeling,” she said. And she says her experience is not so unique, as space applications are quickly opening up access for all of us. “Everyday people can also look up to [space] and see it as their access, and their accessibility,” she said. “In previous space programs, it’s this huge division of how normal people get into space. In 2018, Bernstein and his cofounders launched Zeno Power. Her first-year summer at the Space Court Foundation (SCF) convinced her she didn’t have to follow the big-law track—she could chart her own path. That path ran straight to the FCC Space Bureau, where she was the Front Office’s first intern during the bureau’s Part 100 licensing overhaul. “I was constantly in awe every single day,” Sugarman said. “They would find just such creative ways to handle a certain issue.” Rules of the range: Sugarman brings that same creativity to her research. candidates.raw_excerpt: Hydrogen may be the most common element in the cosmos, but scientists could use it to do something unique: uncover the nature of dark energy, the mysterious force driving the accelerating expansion of the universe. This new line of dark energy investigation comes from the fact that researchers have determined that the CHIME (Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) project can detect the faint radio glow of hydrogen from the universe's distant past. Not only does this represent a faster and much less expensive way to investigate dark energy, but it is a major milestone for CHIME. The instrument was specifically devised to investigate dark energy and its pervasive influence. "This is a completely new technique for probing the cosmos, delivered by an instrument that was conceived and built by Canadians," CHIME principal investigator Mark Halpern of the University of British Columbia said in a statement . "It's a bold new step in the global cosmology program and a Canadian success story." Why is dark energy so problematic? Dark energy is the mysterious force that is accelerating the expansion of the universe . It is so problematic for scientists because it started acting on the fabric of space only after the expansion triggered by the Big Bang had halted. That's akin to pushing a child on a swing, watching it stop, and then seeing the swing start up again without a push. And, not only that, but the swing starts oscillating faster and faster. Consider scientists akin to very worried parents, who would really like to know where this ghostly push came from and how it is going to proceed. Just as, if the push on the swing continues, the child could end up in the bushes, or in orbit, the strengthening of dark energy could result in the cold death of the cosmos, or even a " Big Rip " scenario that sees space shredded. Alternatively, if it weakens and allows gravity to reassert dominance, then the universe could collapse back in on itself, resulting in a " Big Crunch "

candidates.title: Astronomers witness supermassive black hole gorge on a cosmic meal before 'burping' radio jets 300 days later
candidates.raw_excerpt: Using the NASA X-ray spacecraft Swift combined with radio observations, astronomers have observed a supermassive black hole burping radio jets 300 days after a heavy cosmic meal. The team was also able to roughly estimate the mass of this feeding cosmic titan, which sits at the heart of the Perseus Cluster, a massive collection of thousands of galaxies. The black hole sits at the center of the galaxy NGC 1275, located around 225 light-years away, and is the brightest galaxy of the Perseus Cluster . The supermassive black hole first flared in X-rays, which indicated an increase in the rate at which it was accreting matter. Actively feeding supermassive black holes sit in regions called active galactic nuclei (AGNs), with their immense gravity heating surrounding matter, causing them to glow brightly. These emissions are boosted by material channeled to the poles of the central black hole, from where it is blasted out as powerful twin jets that shine across the electromagnetic spectrum , particularly in radio waves. The observation of the following radio jet from the AGN at the heart of NGC 1275 via flaring in radio waves is crucial for understanding the relationship between the disk of matter that surrounds and feeds the black hole, called an accretion disk, and the jets it launches. This so-called disk-jet coupling is key to developing a better picture of how black holes influence star formation in the galaxies in which they sit, and thus the growth of those galaxies. Making these observations is no mean feat. The ideal spacecraft for observing X-ray emissions is Chandra , but it doesn't observe NGC 1275 frequently enough to observe its long-term behaviour. NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory may lack the power of Chandra, but having launched in 2004, it has collected a vast amount of data regarding NGC 1275 and its central supermassive black hole. candidates.title: The moon could turn astronauts into 'walking, high voltage capacitors' that accidentally zap spacecraft
candidates.raw_excerpt: NASA is asking for ideas to stop static electricity from zapping astronauts or critical hardware during moon missions. The agency opened a "Lunar Grounding Challenge" to avoid situations where an astronaut on the moon could become "a walking, high voltage capacitor." Submissions for the $150,000 competition are due Jan. 15 and you can see the requirements here . NASA is hoping to put astronaut boots at the lunar south pole in 2028 during the Artemis 4 or 5 missions, on the first landing mission since NASA's Apollo 17 in 1972. But simulations suggest that both "tribocharging" (electric-charge transfer between two objects) and plasma charging (from ambient gas in the region) could build up electric charge on spacesuits. "This problem is severely compounded when entering lunar shadows and permanently shadowed regions," the agency wrote, referring to deeply cratered areas where the sun does not touch the lunar surface. The concern is that astronauts' spacesuits could become electrically charged, as there would be an excess of electrons (negatively charged particles) compared with ions (positively charged) in these areas. "The risk occurs when an astronaut returns to the spacecraft," the agency added. The lander would have a slight positive charge, producing an issue once the "highly negatively-charged astronaut approaches the vehicle." NASA has asked industry partners for ideas that can help an astronaut avoid "becoming a walking, high voltage capacitor", including issues such as an electrical arc that could damage spacesuits, spark fires in the oxygen atmosphere of a spacecraft, or create electrical shocks. candidates.title: The 'Halloween Fireballs' are coming. Here's what to expect from the Taurids this year
candidates.raw_excerpt: They don't produce anything like the torrent of "shooting stars" associated with August's Perseids or December's Geminids, but the Taurid meteor showers have something else going for them — fireballs. The Taurids are famous for occasionally producing exceptionally bright, slow-moving meteors that can streak dramatically across the night sky from September to December. As a bonus, they're visible from both the Northern and Southern hemispheres. That's because they appear to emanate from the constellation Taurus, which sits close to the ecliptic, the apparent path the sun takes across the sky as Earth orbits around it. The Taurids are actually two closely related showers — the Southern Taurids and Northern Taurids — whose activity overlaps in late October and November. That's why they're known informally by skywatchers as the "Halloween fireballs." The broad overlapping peaks make the Taurids less about watching on one particular night and more about keeping an eye on the night sky for several weeks. Both have their radiant points — the place in the night sky where their "shooting stars" appear to come from — close to the famous Pleiades (M45) open cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus . There's another tempting reason to watch the Taurids in 2026 — moonlight will cause little interference around the main peaks. When are the Southern Taurids? The Southern Taurids are already underway. According to the American Meteor Society , they're active from Sept. 20 through Nov. 20, with two distinct components. The annual component peaks around Oct. 14, while a component particularly associated with fireballs peaks overnight on Nov. 4-5. That's the night to circle if you're hoping to see one of the "Halloween Fireballs." However, don't expect a conventional meteor storm . The Southern Taurids have an average zenithal hourly rate of about five meteors per hour. Etosha National Park in northern Namibia hosts the largest salt pan, or piece of land covered with salt and other minerals, in the country. This image of the Etosha Pan was captured on April 5 of this year by Europe's Copernicus Sentinel-2 mission, which consists of two identical satellites in the same orbit. The Sentinel-2 pair observe and capture imagery of our planet in different wavelengths using a high-resolution multispectral imager that can see 13 different spectral bands, or ranges of wavelengths. By looking at our planet from space, and observing it through different wavelengths and colors, we can better understand Earth's topography and how it changes over time. candidates.title: Jurassic fossil reveals early mammaliaform adaptations
candidates.raw_excerpt:
An international research team led by Shenyang Normal University has discovered and named Megacauda sungei, the largest known Jurassic docodont mammaliaform. The fossil was found in Jurassic rock formations dating back about 160 million years in Ningcheng County, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. The study was published online in Nature on October 7.

The fossil, housed at the Liaoning Paleontological Museum of Shenyang Normal University, measures about 52 centimeters in length and weighs an estimated 1 to 2 kilograms. It preserves a well-defined skull, a robust torso and a long tail.

The discovery sheds light on the diversity and evolution of Jurassic mammaliaforms, an extinct group that includes modern mammals and their extinct relatives. The specimen's well-preserved throat anatomy and hyoid bones resemble those of modern mammals. These features suggest that the anatomical structures involved in swallowing and suckling had evolved in early mammaliaforms long before modern mammals emerged, according to Li Yikun, associate professor at Shenyang Normal University's School of Paleontology and the study's first author.

The fossil also preserves much of the pelvis, hind limbs and tail vertebrae. Together with its distinctive teeth, these features suggest that Megacauda sungei was adapted to a semiaquatic lifestyle. Its prominent upper canine teeth and shearing cheek teeth indicate that it preyed on small animals, potentially including aquatic prey.
